SUBLEASE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Alex Lee

PARTIES AND PROPERTY
This is a sublease agreement between Jordan Alex Lee ("Sublessor") and Morgan Lee ("Subtenant") for the property (or portion of the property) at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield. Sublessor is the tenant under an existing lease with Acme Properties, LLC ("Landlord") covering that property (the "Master Lease"). The sublease term runs from September 1, 2026 to February 28, 2027. This sublease is subject and subordinate to the Master Lease, and does not change, replace, or release any of Sublessor's obligations to Landlord under the Master Lease.

RENT
Subtenant will pay Sublessor rent of $1,800 per month, due on the _______ day of each month, payable by: _______________________________________________. This sublease rent is separate from, and does not replace or reduce, the rent Sublessor owes Landlord under the Master Lease.

WHAT GOVERNS SUBLESSOR'S RIGHT TO SUBLET
California has a statutory chapter specifically addressing a landlord's ability to restrict a tenant from transferring the tenant's lease interest (by assignment or sublease), including a default rule that if the lease requires the landlord's consent but states no standard for it, that consent may not be unreasonably withheld. That chapter, by its own terms, applies only to a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. For a residential tenancy, whether Jordan Alex Lee may sublet 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield to Morgan Lee, and whether Acme Properties, LLC's consent is required first, is controlled by the terms of the existing lease between Acme Properties, LLC and Jordan Alex Lee (the "Master Lease") — not by that separate statutory chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This chapter applies to transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease of real property for other than residential purposes."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.010 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the assignment/sublease restrictions chapter is nonresidential-only (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.010.)
  "“Lease” means a lease or sublease of real property for other than residential purposes, and includes modifications and other agreements affecting a lease."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, "lease" is defined as nonresidential for this chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.020.)
  "(a) The Legislature finds and declares: (1) It is the public policy of the state and fundamental to the commerce and economic development of the state to enable and facilitate freedom of contract by the parties to commercial real property leases. (2) The parties to commercial real property leases must be able to negotiate and conduct their affairs in reasonable reliance on the rights and protections given them under the laws of the state. (3) Until the case of Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal. 3d 488 (1985), and its predecessor, Cohen v. Ratinoff, 147 Cal. App. 3d 321 (1983), the parties to commercial real property leases could reasonably rely on the law of the state to provide that if a lease restriction requires the landlord’s consent for transfer of the tenant’s interest in the lease but provides no standard for giving or withholding consent, the landlord’s consent may be unreasonably withheld."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.270(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, legislative findings confirming the chapter concerns commercial real property leases (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.270.)
  "We are presented only with a commercial lease and therefore do not address the question whether residential leases are controlled by the principles articulated in this opinion."
  — Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.1 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, expressly declining to decide whether its commercial-lease rule extends to residential leases (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1282333/kendall-v-ernest-pestana-inc/)
  Known gap: This is a real, easy-to-miss gap rather than an assumption forced to fit: Civil Code Chapter 6 (Assignment and Sublease, §§ 1995.010-1995.340) — including its default rule that an unstandardized landlord-consent requirement may not be unreasonably withheld — is defined, by its own text, to cover only a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. There is no parallel Civil Code chapter creating a general residential right to sublet or a residential landlord-consent standard. That means a residential tenant's subletting rights genuinely are, in the main, a matter of what the Master Lease itself says: a typical residential lease either bars subletting outright, allows it only with the landlord's prior written consent, or is silent (in which case older common-law principles about a tenant's default freedom to transfer a leasehold interest can come into play). This document does not assume the Master Lease permits or forbids subletting, or that it requires consent — that has to be checked directly against the Master Lease's own text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope of California's assignment/subletting statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. The first two citations are sections of the same statutory chapter (§§ 1995.010, 1995.020) defining that chapter's own scope; the third citation, § 1995.270's legislative findings, is an independent statutory source that separately corroborates the chapter's commercial-only focus and its historical basis in the Kendall v. Ernest Pestana litigation. The fourth citation goes further still: it's Kendall's own text (verified directly against CourtListener's opinion record, not a paraphrase), and in a footnote the California Supreme Court itself expressly declined to say whether the commercial-lease consent principles it was announcing in that case apply to residential leases at all — meaning even the single most important California case on landlord-consent standards pointedly leaves the residential question open, rather than answering it.

ASSIGNMENT VS. SUBLEASE
Subletting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield to Morgan Lee is legally different from assigning the Master Lease to Morgan Lee, even though both are ways Jordan Alex Lee can transfer some interest in the leased property to someone else. In a sublease, Jordan Alex Lee transfers only part of its remaining interest under the Master Lease — for example, a shorter term than what remains, or only part of the space — and remains a tenant to Acme Properties, LLC while also taking on a landlord-like role toward Morgan Lee. In a full assignment, Jordan Alex Lee would instead transfer its entire remaining interest under the Master Lease to the new party, who would then generally deal with Acme Properties, LLC directly going forward in Jordan Alex Lee's place. This document is a sublease, not an assignment: Jordan Alex Lee keeps its position as tenant under the Master Lease and remains directly responsible to Acme Properties, LLC for compliance with it, as described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Since the present case involves an assignment rather than a sublease, we will speak primarily in terms of assignments. However, our holding applies equally to subleases. The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease."
  — Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, the assignment/sublease distinction stated directly (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1282333/kendall-v-ernest-pestana-inc/)
  "The generally stated distinction between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the entire unexpired term. ... [W]e are committed to the so-called Massachusetts rule that where the transferor reserves the right of reentry for breach of conditions he has a "contingent reversionary interest" which prevents his transfer from operating as an assignment of the whole of the unexpired term. Instead, a sublease arises."
  — Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, independently stating the same distinction and its doctrinal basis (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1126371/hartman-ranch-co-v-associated-oil-co/)
  "(a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (e) “Transfer” of a tenant’s interest in a lease means an assignment, sublease, or other voluntary or involuntary transfer or encumbrance of all or part of a tenant’s interest in the lease."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, "transfer" is defined to include both assignment and sublease as distinct categories, and a sublease creates a "sublandlord" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.020.)
  Known gap: This distinction is confirmed directly against primary case text, not a secondary-source paraphrase. Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2, states it in so many words: "The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease." Kendall cites, for that same point, Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 — an independent, older California Supreme Court decision (about an oil-and-gas lease, not real estate generally) that states the distinction on its own terms and explains the doctrine behind it: California follows the "Massachusetts rule" that a transferor who reserves a right of reentry for breach of conditions keeps a "contingent reversionary interest," which is what keeps the transfer from operating as a full assignment of the unexpired term — a sublease results instead. Both quotes below were read directly from each case's opinion text (via CourtListener), not assumed from a secondary summary. Neither case involved a residential tenancy — Kendall was a commercial hangar-space dispute and Hartman Ranch an oil-and-gas lease dispute — but the assignment/sublease distinction itself is treated in both opinions as general property-law doctrine rather than something specific to a commercial lease, and Civil Code § 1995.020(e) (part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above) independently confirms that California statutory law also recognizes assignment and sublease as distinct categories of lease transfer, even though it doesn't itself spell out the substantive test. That third citation quotes two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1995.020(a) and (e) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources, so the real independent authority for the doctrinal test itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as corroboration that California law recognizes the two categories at all. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual doctrinal test — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific document.

SUBLESSOR REMAINS BOUND TO LANDLORD
Entering into this sublease with Morgan Lee does not release Jordan Alex Lee from any of its obligations to Acme Properties, LLC under the Master Lease. Jordan Alex Lee remains fully responsible to Acme Properties, LLC for rent, upkeep, and all other Master Lease obligations for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, regardless of whether Morgan Lee pays rent on time, complies with the Master Lease's terms, or vacates early. If Morgan Lee breaches this sublease or damages the property, Jordan Alex Lee — not Acme Properties, LLC — bears that loss in the first instance, unless Jordan Alex Lee separately recovers it from Morgan Lee. At the same time, under this sublease Jordan Alex Lee effectively stands in Acme Properties, LLC's shoes toward Morgan Lee, taking on landlord-like responsibilities to Morgan Lee while remaining, itself, a tenant to Acme Properties, LLC.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The lessor's interests are also protected by the fact that the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease. (Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 [328 P.2d 953, 74 A.L.R.2d 1]; Samuels v. Ottinger (1915) 169 Cal. 209, 212 [146 P. 638].)"
  — Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 500 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, original tenant remains liable as a surety after transferring the lease (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1282333/kendall-v-ernest-pestana-inc/)
  "Ordinarily an assignment of a lease does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment. ... Nor does the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease affect the liability of the lessee to the lessor. ... but as between the lessor and the lessee the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent."
  — Peiser v. Mettler, 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 (1958) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, independently stating the original tenant remains a primary obligor to the landlord (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1181332/peiser-v-mettler/)
  "(a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (d) “Tenant” includes a subtenant or assignee."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a sublessor is both a "tenant" to the landlord and a "sublandlord" (landlord) to the subtenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.020.)
  Known gap: This is a well-established rule of California landlord-tenant law, confirmed directly against primary case text. The California Supreme Court has stated it plainly: "the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease" (Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 500) — a sentence that itself cites, for that exact point, two of the Supreme Court's own earlier decisions, so the underlying rule rests on at least three independent sources, not one restated citation. One of those two, Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602, was independently pulled and confirms the rule in even more direct language (quoting an earlier case, De Hart v. Allen): an assignment or sublease "does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment," and "the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease" doesn't change that, because "as between the lessor and the lessee[,] the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent." All of this case law states the rule in the assignment context specifically, but nothing in the reasoning turns on the assignment/sublease distinction described elsewhere in this document — a sublessor, who transfers only part of the leasehold interest and keeps an ongoing tenancy relationship with the landlord, has at least as much of a continuing contractual relationship with the landlord as an assignor does, so the same primary-obligor/surety-liability logic applies with equal or greater force to a sublease. Separately, Civil Code § 1995.020(a), (d) — part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above — independently corroborates the underlying structure by defining a sublessor as simultaneously a "tenant" to the original landlord and a "sublandlord" to the subtenant, consistent with the sublessor's obligations to the landlord surviving the sublease. That statutory citation likewise quotes two subsections of the same section, § 1995.020(a) and (d) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources; the independent authority for the liability rule itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as structural corroboration. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual liability rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease — and it says nothing about whatever separate indemnity or reimbursement rights Sublessor may or may not have against Subtenant; the actual Master Lease's own default and remedies provisions, not this general default description, control the mechanics of any actual dispute.

SUBTENANT HAS NO DIRECT RELATIONSHIP WITH LANDLORD
As a general default rule, Morgan Lee does not step into a direct legal relationship with Acme Properties, LLC merely by virtue of this sublease. Morgan Lee's rights and obligations run to Jordan Alex Lee, not to Acme Properties, LLC, and Acme Properties, LLC's remedies for a breach of the Master Lease generally run against Jordan Alex Lee, not directly against Morgan Lee. This sublease does not, by itself, give Morgan Lee the right to enforce the Master Lease against Acme Properties, LLC, or give Acme Properties, LLC the right to collect rent or otherwise enforce lease terms directly against Morgan Lee for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, unless the Master Lease, Acme Properties, LLC's written consent to this sublease, or a separate agreement signed by all three parties provides otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Defendant contends that as a sublessee it is not liable to the original lessor in damages for breach of covenants in the parent lease. This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term."
  — Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, a subtenant is liable only to the sublessor, not the original landlord (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1126371/hartman-ranch-co-v-associated-oil-co/)
  "An assignee in possession is liable to the parent lessor by virtue of privity of estate (covenants running with the land), and it is not ordinarily necessary to consider whether by virtue of an agreement of assumption there is also privity of contract between them. But where the assignee is no longer in possession, the privity of estate is terminated ..., and if he is liable to the lessor it is by virtue of his contract of assumption. Since as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession there is no privity of estate with the lessor, cases involving an assignee who has assumed the parent lease, but is no longer in possession, will indicate the rule applicable also to sublessees who assume the parent lease."
  — Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 244 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, a subtenant lacks privity of estate with the original landlord (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1126371/hartman-ranch-co-v-associated-oil-co/)
  "Whatever remedies the lessor of any real property has against his immediate lessee for the breach of any agreement in the lease, or for recovery of the possession, he has against the assignees of the lessee, for any cause of action accruing while they are such assignees, except where the assignment is made by way of security for a loan, and is not accompanied by possession of the premises."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 822 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a landlord's lease remedies extend to the tenant's "assignees" — subtenants are not mentioned (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=822.)
  Known gap: This no-privity default is a real, well-established rule of California property law, confirmed directly against primary case text. Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242, states it directly: "This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term." A few pages later the same opinion explains the doctrinal mechanism — that the sublessee's relationship with the original landlord lacks privity of estate (the property-law relationship that, for an assignee in full possession, makes the assignee directly answerable to the landlord on the lease covenants): "as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession[,] there is no privity of estate with the lessor." Both quotes below are from the same 1937 case rather than independently authored sources; that case is, however, corroborated by a second, independent source: Civil Code § 822 extends a landlord's lease remedies — for breach of a lease agreement, or for recovery of possession — expressly to the tenant's "assignees," but its text never mentions subtenants or sublessees at all, which is consistent with (though not itself an express statement of) the same no-privity default for subtenants that Hartman Ranch states directly. Hartman Ranch was an oil-and-gas lease dispute, not a residential tenancy, but the privity principle it applies is general California property-law doctrine rather than something specific to that lease type. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual default rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. Nothing here should be read as guaranteeing that no direct relationship can ever arise in a particular deal — a landlord's written consent to a sublease, a separate non-disturbance or attornment agreement, or specific master lease language can each create direct rights or obligations between the landlord and the subtenant, and the actual Master Lease and any consent documents should be checked for that possibility.

MASTER LEASE COMPLIANCE AND LANDLORD CONSENT
☐ Sublessor has obtained Landlord's prior written consent to this sublease, as required by the Master Lease, and a copy of that written consent is attached.
☐ Sublessor has reviewed the Master Lease and confirmed it does not require Landlord's consent to sublet.
☐ Landlord's consent is being requested and this sublease does not take effect until it is received.

A copy of the Master Lease (or its provisions governing subletting, use of the premises, and other tenant obligations) is attached as Exhibit A. Subtenant agrees to comply with those Master Lease provisions to the extent they apply to Subtenant's use of the property, and a violation of the Master Lease by Subtenant is also a breach of this sublease.

SIGNATURES
Signed:

Sublessor: _______________________ Date: _______________
Subtenant: _______________________ Date: _______________

Landlord's consent (if required by the Master Lease):
Landlord: _______________________ Date: _______________

(1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242, states it directly: "This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term." A few pages later the same opinion explains the doctrinal mechanism — that the sublessee's relationship with the original landlord lacks privity of estate (the property-law relationship that, for an assignee in full possession, makes the assignee directly answerable to the landlord on the lease covenants): "as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession[,] there is no privity of estate with the lessor." Both quotes below are from the same 1937 case rather than independently authored sources; that case is, however, corroborated by a second, independent source: Civil Code § 822 extends a landlord's lease remedies — for breach of a lease agreement, or for recovery of possession — expressly to the tenant's "assignees," but its text never mentions subtenants or sublessees at all, which is consistent with (though not itself an express statement of) the same no-privity default for subtenants that Hartman Ranch states directly. Hartman Ranch was an oil-and-gas lease dispute, not a residential tenancy, but the privity principle it applies is general California property-law doctrine rather than something specific to that lease type. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual default rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease.
